The vessel, operated as part of the university's sailing program, was carrying four students and two safety officers when it suddenly overturned amid rough conditions on the water. In the chaos of the capsizing, the crew found themselves with only four life jackets to share among six people—a shortfall that would test their resourcefulness and resolve in the hours that followed.

According to accounts from survivors, the group made the decision to stay together rather than risk separating in the open water. Clinging to one another and to pieces of debris from the capsized vessel, they endured swells, fatigue, dehydration, and the psychological strain of not knowing whether help would arrive in time. The ordeal stretched on for more than a day, with the crew rotating use of the limited life jackets and relying on each other for physical and emotional support to stay afloat.

At the center of the tragedy was safety officer Roger Stone, whose actions in the vessel's final, chaotic moments are being credited with saving multiple lives. As the boat went down, Stone worked to push several of the students and crew members to safety through a hatch, ensuring they had a chance to escape the sinking vessel. In doing so, he was unable to save himself.

"Roger Stone gave his life so that others could live," said a Texas A&M official in a statement following the rescue. "His final act was one of selflessness and courage that embodies everything we hope to instill in the people who serve in these safety roles. He is, without question, a hero."

Survivors echoed that sentiment, describing Stone's actions as instrumental to their escape from the capsizing vessel. Without his intervention in those critical moments, several of them said, they likely would not have made it out of the hull before the boat went under.

Once in the water, the remaining five survivors—four students and one safety officer—faced a grueling test of endurance. Battling exhaustion and the constant threat of losing consciousness or slipping beneath the waves, the group held onto one another through the night and into the following day. Rescuers who eventually located the group described their survival as a testament to sheer determination.

"These young people and their fellow crew member displayed an absolutely fierce will to live," one rescue official said. "To stay together, to keep each other going for over 24 hours in those conditions with limited flotation equipment—that takes an extraordinary amount of strength, both physical and mental."

All five remaining survivors were pulled from the water alive and have since received medical attention. Texas A&M University has expressed both grief over the loss of Roger Stone and profound relief and gratitude for the survival of the others involved in the incident.

The university indicated that a full review of the sailing program's safety protocols would be conducted in the wake of the accident, including an examination of life jacket availability and emergency procedures for future training exercises. In the meantime, the campus community has rallied around the survivors and mourned the loss of Stone, whose sacrifice has already begun to shape the legacy of this harrowing chapter in the program's history.

The Coast Guard said it received a distress call Tuesday afternoon reporting that a sailboat had capsized approximately 20 miles off the Texas coast amid deteriorating weather conditions, including high winds and rough seas.

"Multiple crew members were in the water when our units arrived on scene," said Coast Guard Petty Officer Marcus Reyes, a spokesperson for Coast Guard Sector Houston-Galveston. "This individual's actions are consistent with what we hear time and again in these situations — a trained professional prioritizing others' survival over their own," Reyes said. "Preliminary reports suggest this officer's efforts were directly responsible for saving multiple young lives."

Coast Guard helicopter and boat crews, along with a nearby commercial vessel that responded to the mayday call, pulled survivors from the water over the course of roughly 90 minutes. "Our university community is devastated by this tragic loss," the statement read. "We are grateful beyond words for the selflessness and heroism shown in the final moments of this individual's life, which we believe prevented further loss of life among our students."

**Coast Guard credits crew's preparation and quick thinking for survival in open water**

Five sailors are recovering after spending 26 harrowing hours adrift in open water following the sudden sinking of their vessel, in an ordeal that ended when the crew used a simple flashlight to flag down a Coast Guard search aircraft flying overhead in the darkness.

The vessel went down rapidly, according to accounts from the survivors, giving the crew little time to do more than activate an emergency beacon and scramble into survival gear before abandoning ship. What followed was more than a full day battling exposure, fatigue, and the psychological strain of uncertainty on open water.

## A Race Against Time

Search and rescue crews were alerted after the vessel's emergency position-indicating radio beacon (EPIRB) transmitted a distress signal, triggering an immediate response. Coast Guard aircraft and surface vessels began combing a wide stretch of ocean, working against fading light, drifting currents, and the diminishing odds that accompany prolonged exposure at sea.

Survival experts note that the first 24 hours after a vessel sinks are typically the most critical. Hypothermia, dehydration, and the sheer psychological toll of isolation can overwhelm even experienced sailors. That the group remained together, conserved energy, and stayed alert enough to signal for help when the moment came is being cited by officials as a key factor in their survival.

## The Flashlight That Made the Difference

As night fell over the search area, a Coast Guard aircraft crew scanning the water below caught an irregular flicker in the darkness — a flashlight beam, aimed skyward by the stranded sailors.

That signal, transmitted with what officials described as a basic handheld flashlight, was enough to draw the aircraft back for a closer pass. Confirming the sighting, the crew relayed coordinates to nearby rescue assets, setting in motion the final phase of an operation that had spanned more than a day.

"In conditions like these, something as simple as a flashlight can be the difference between a rescue and a tragedy," a Coast Guard spokesperson said, emphasizing how essential basic signaling equipment remains even in an era of satellite technology and electronic beacons.

## Rescue and Recovery

Once located, the five survivors were retrieved from the water and transported to safety, where they were assessed for exposure, dehydration, and fatigue. Coast Guard officials reported that all five were in stable condition given the circumstances, a testament both to their physical endurance and the swift execution of the rescue once contact was established.

Details about the cause of the sinking remain under review, though officials noted that the presence of working emergency equipment — including the EPIRB and the flashlight that ultimately proved decisive — played an outsized role in the outcome.

## A Reminder of the Sea's Unpredictability

The incident serves as a stark reminder of how quickly conditions at sea can turn catastrophic, and how critical basic preparedness remains even in an age of advanced maritime technology.
